content: Each year, approximately 6 million children under the age of 5 die worldwide. This tragic loss results in an estimated 20% reduction in adult productivity within their respective countries. Health services, healthcare workers, and community providers play a critical role in fostering the development of young children. The early years of a child’s life are crucial for their overall development. This period presents significant opportunities for growth but also leaves children vulnerable to negative influences. Many children, particularly those living in extreme poverty in developing countries, fail to reach their full potential due to inadequate nutrition, insufficient care, and limited opportunities for learning. However, these children and their families can be supported through targeted interventions. Providing children with proper nutrition, healthcare, consistent loving care, and encouragement to learn during their early years significantly improves their outcomes. These children are more likely to perform better in school, enjoy better health, achieve higher earnings, and contribute more actively to society. This is especially vital for children living in poverty. A strong foundation in early childhood not only benefits the individual throughout their lifetime but also positively impacts the next generation. The Care for Child Development package includes several components designed to support families and improve child development. These include simple recommendations for families provided by healthcare workers, training materials for health and community workers, problem-solving support for families, advocacy materials, and a framework for monitoring and evaluation. This initiative, developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF, aims to promote the cognitive, language, and social-emotional development of young children through play and communication. It is particularly focused on reaching the most disadvantaged children and families. When implemented on a large scale, this program can yield significant public health and social benefits. Educated and healthy individuals contribute to the financial and social wealth of their societies. Recognizing this, WHO, UNICEF, and their partners have developed materials to assist families in fostering the development of young children. Improving early childhood care is fundamental to achieving global development goals, such as the Millennium Development Goals. Research has shown that over 200 million children in developing countries—more than one-third of all children—fail to reach their developmental potential due to poverty, poor nutrition, and limited learning opportunities. These disadvantages often stem from families living in poverty. The WHO’s Commission on the Social Determinants of Health highlights the importance of early childhood development for equity, adult health, well-being, and productivity. Similarly, the Education for All Global Monitoring Report (2007) emphasizes that better early childhood care improves primary school performance. The World Bank’s poverty reduction strategies also prioritize early childhood development. Furthermore, the United Nations Secretary-General’s Study on Violence against Children identifies the importance of improved care for young children in reducing violence, as young children often bear the brunt of parental violence. There is strong evidence that brain development is most rapid during the early years of life. When children lack adequate stimulation, support, and nurturing, their development is severely affected. However, early interventions for disadvantaged children can improve survival, health, growth, and cognitive and social development. Children who receive early assistance are more likely to succeed in school. Efforts to enhance early childhood development are not merely costs but investments, with cost-benefit analyses showing returns of 4 to 5 times the amount invested, and in some cases, even higher. The healthcare system has a unique opportunity to support early childhood development. Health services often reach more young children and their families than other services, particularly through home-visiting programs. Good nutrition and health are essential for children’s development, and healthcare services must leverage their reach to strengthen families’ efforts in promoting child development. The United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child calls for all countries to enable children to reach their full potential and to support families in this process. This includes advocating for children’s rights to development in addition to survival. There is now substantial evidence on how children’s development can be promoted through healthcare-related activities in developing countries. The Care for Child Development intervention is based on the best available evidence and focuses on critical caregiver skills, such as sensitivity and responsiveness, which are essential for healthy growth and development. Research shows that these skills can be taught to caregivers. Families, as the primary supporters of children’s growth and development, often need guidance to focus on the most impactful activities, such as play and communication. The Care for Child Development program provides this guidance and can be implemented effectively to benefit children and families worldwide.
